title: Learning Outcome
inspectionNotes: Five outcome bullets: redundant/closed chains, actuation/transmission/selection, stiffness/compliance, position/force sensing, mobile manipulation workspace/trajectory/kinematics.

title: Redundant & Closed-chain Structures - Micromanipulators
inspectionNotes: Redundancy stated as more than six DOF for full spatial pose; closed loops; distal fast precise micromanipulator DOFs; extra joints help singularity/collision avoidance. The universal 6-DOF finite-solutions and 7-DOF infinite-solutions-for-any-pose claims require reachable regular poses, rank/task/limits qualifiers. Redundancy is task-relative, not always n>6.

title: Closed-loop structures
inspectionNotes: Closed-loop versus serial topology; Motoman L-3 joints2/3 named; increased stiffness versus generally smaller joint range/workspace. Right schematic labels moving end-effector upper platform, base below and dashed closed-loop route; three drawn struts illustrate topology, not proof of six actuators or a Motoman L-3 image.

title: The Stewart Mechanism
inspectionNotes: Six linear actuators connect base and moving platform; each leg base universal joint2DOF, platform spherical joint3DOF. Fully parallel6DOF, easy inverse length computation versus complex forward pose recovery, high stiffness/load capacity and limited workspace. Right photo shows actual six-leg platform. Inverse length derived as norm(p+Rbi−ai), not printed; “often no closed-form” not a categorical impossibility.

title: Grübler’s Formula
inspectionNotes: Exact formula F=6(l−n−1)+Σ fi. l counts links including ground; n counts joints. Counts six universal2DOF, six spherical3DOF, six prismatic1DOF, n18. The formula assumes independent generic constraints; singular/special overconstrained cases need rank analysis. Photo repeats the platform, no new dimensions.

title: Stewart Mechanism Example (Continued)
inspectionNotes: Twelve actuator links (two rigid members per telescoping actuator), one base, one platform =>l14. Sum fi12+18+6=36. F=6(14−18−1)+36=6. Continued photo no new geometry; numerical derivation is substantive incremental content.

title: Actuation Schemes - Actuator location
inspectionNotes: Integrated motor, reducer and transmission design; effects on dynamic performance, control and structure. Local direct drive: actuator at/near joint output attached directly; remote drive toward base away from driven joint. Proximity alone is not sufficient to call a geared motor direct drive; use stated direct-output connection.

title: Reduction and transmission systems
inspectionNotes: Spur, bevel, worm, cross-helical gears named and pictured (photos are unlabelled individually); backlash/friction; tighter mesh trades less backlash for more friction. η>1 is speed-reduction ratio, not efficiency. ωo=ωi/η and τo=ητi require ideal lossless magnitudes or consistent sign convention; actual friction acknowledged above makes unconditional exact torque equation incomplete.

title: Flexible Bands, Cables, and Belts
inspectionNotes: Remote transmission and possible reduction; flexibility proportional to element length under unchanged material/section; tension-only requires preload or opposing active drive. Toothed belts and roller chains described as stiffer/compact, chains around smaller pulleys (qualitative comparisons need fixed design basis). Diagram small input r1 left, larger output r2 right, open belt; η=r2/r1, no slip implied, opposite ratio would be speedup.

title: Lead Screws and Ball-Bearing Screws
inspectionNotes: Rotary-to-linear conversion. Left drawing direct lead-screw/nut thread contact labelled Nut; right drawing balls between threads labelled Race. Lead screws stiff/high load/high friction; ball screw recirculating bearings reduce friction and are typically backdrivable, not always self-locking. No lead/pitch equation printed; derived kinematics only if explicitly supplied.

title: Stiffness and Deflections
inspectionNotes: Structural and drivetrain stiffness important. Source says most industrial robots infer tool pose via forward kinematics of sensed joint positions; do not present survey claim as timeless fact. Compliance yields sag under gravity/load and rigid-model pose error; flexibility produces resonances limiting dynamic performance/control bandwidth. Encoders alone may miss unmodelled link deformation.

title: Flexible elements in parallel and series
inspectionNotes: Parallel k=k1+k2; series1/k=1/k1+1/k2; compliance reciprocal. For reduction stages in series, stiffness/compliance must first be referred to the same coordinate/shaft using p592; raw numbers on different shafts cannot be directly summed. Scalar linear-spring model, positive k, common generalized coordinate.

title: Stiffness and Deflections – Shafts and Gears
inspectionNotes: Solid round shaft torsional k=Gπd^4/(32l), d diameter not radius, l length G shear modulus. Gear output stiffness with input fixed k=Cg b r², b face width r output radius Cg material constant. Both rotational units N·m/rad, not N/m. Shaft and gear photos contain no dimensions; avoid inferring tooth counts. Formula assumes uniform linear-elastic solid shaft; hollow shaft needs polar difference not supplied.

title: Stiffness and Deflections Belts and Links
inspectionNotes: Exact equations ko=η²ki for ideal reduction η>1; belt axial k=AE/l; hollow round cantilever end-load stiffness3πE(do^4−di^4)/(64l³); hollow square E(wo^4−wi^4)/(4l³). Belt schematic right; cantilever clamped left with downward tip-region load. Distinguish rotational transformed k from translational belt/beam k. Assumptions small linear elastic deflection, constant section, correct end-load boundary; do>di>=0, wo>wi>=0. Formulas check as3EI/l³.

title: Electric Motors
inspectionNotes: Electric motors easy interface/precision; qualitative power-weight comparison with fluids; DC brushed motor stationary brushes feed rotor windings through rotating commutator. Winding overheating major limit; torque proportional current for constant flux/linear model. Generic motor cutaway at upper right does not explicitly show labelled brushes/commutator, so do not identify DC topology from photo alone.

title: Position Sensing
inspectionNotes: Servo control uses desired-minus-sensed joint position error to generate force/torque command. Co-located sensor at actuator shaft is recommended. “Most effective” not a universal end-effector-accuracy guarantee; shaft sensing can miss downstream compliance p589. No sensor hardware diagram. Modern-industry prevalence claims should be source-attributed.

title: Force Sensing
inspectionNotes: Strain-gauge contact force sensors: bonded to metal, output proportional strain in calibrated range. Design count/placement/stiffness/sensitivity/overload; positions actuator/wrist/fingertips; wrist3–6 wrench components. Photo shows cylindrical transducer and enlarged serpentine bonded foil gauge with two leads; do not infer total gauge count or six-axis capability from one pictured gauge. Not all possible force sensors use gauges; scope to illustrated class.

title: Force Sensor Design Issues
inspectionNotes: Flexure deflection creates stiffness-versus-sensitivity tradeoff; limit stops protect overload; minimizing welded/bolted joints near flexures reduces hysteresis (does not prove eliminates all hysteresis). Differential measurements improve linearity and reject shared temperature/off-axis effects under suitable arrangement, not all arbitrary differential pairs. Foil more durable/lower sensitivity; semiconductor higher sensitivity/more overload vulnerability; comparison as given.

title: Mobile Robots
inspectionNotes: Interdisciplinary mechanical/electrical/electronics/computer/cognitive/social sciences; autonomous mobility focus versus fixed arms; multiple competence layers; kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI, probability. title: Locomotion
inspectionNotes: Locomotion moves robot by forces against environment; source contrasts fixed-arm object manipulation. title: Wheeled Mobile Robots

Design focus traction/stability/maneuverability/control. Photo has four wheels and payload; no kinematic drive identification justified.

inspectionNotes: Left exact-model loop uses sensed q,qdot in M,V,G,F; right model inputs are desired acceleration/velocity/position and directly adds torque-domain Kp E+Kv Edot. inspectionNotes: Printed Eddot+M(q)^−1 Kv Edot+M(q)^−1 Kp E=0. Faster separate/offline model for known trajectory; not completely decoupled; poles depend on configuration. title: Dual-rate computation split
inspectionNotes: Slow nonlinear dynamic model background process, fast servo/error feedback. No fixed frequency/ratio specified. Footer 10.

title: Dual-rate block diagram
inspectionNotes: Configuration-space diagram: desired acceleration+Kp position error+Kv velocity error pass through M(theta); additive B(theta)+C(theta) and G(theta) feed torque sum. Red ellipse encloses B+C and G, not M, arrow to Computed by background Process. Actual theta feeds M,B+C,G via dashed paths; actual theta dot feeds B+C. B/C individually undefined here; do not invent decomposition formula or assume all model blocks highlighted. Footer 11.

title: Disturbance error coupling and equilibrium
inspectionNotes: Diagram subtracts tau_d at arm input. Therefore positive M^-1 tau_d on E dynamics is consistent E=desired-actual. SSE Kp^-1 M^-1 tau_d assumes constant disturbance, equilibrium, invertibility. Non-diagonal inertia permits cross-joint effects; not necessarily every joint every configuration. Footer 12.

title: Estimated versus actual dynamic model
inspectionNotes: Hat M,V,G,F versus true values; controller alpha=hatM,beta=hatV+hatG+hatF. Exact displayed residual hatM^-1[(M-hatM)qddot+(V-hatV)+(G-hatG)+(F-hatF)] is algebraically consistent; contains actual acceleration, not desired. Perfect-model residual zero; generic mismatch loses decoupling, not universal failure. Footer 13.

title: Industrial joint-control rationale
inspectionNotes: Source claims many/most industrial arms use simple robust almost independent joints, compute/model knowledge/good-enough cost-benefit. Photo illustrative no model-dependent engineering data. Treat prevalence as course statement, not current market survey. Footer 14.

title: Individual-joint PID
inspectionNotes: Alpha=I,beta=0; displayed tauprime=qddot_d+Kv Edot+Kp E+Ki integralE, qddot_d often set0 because unavailable. Diagonal gains/no model compensation. Diagram parallel P,D,I branches plus encoder negative feedback. Dimensional omission: alpha=I maps torque command but unit coefficient desired angular acceleration cannot add to SI torque unless inertia/normalization supplied. Scope numeric tasks qddot_d=0 and torque-domain gains. Footer 15.

title: Joint-control limits and gravity compensation
inspectionNotes: No exact decoupling; interactions and imperfect disturbance rejection, posture-varying damping so average gains. Adds hatG to PID/desired acceleration law. Gravity creates SSE blanket claim requires qualification: ideal stable unsaturated integral action can supply constant gravity with zero final E; PD has finite E. Same acceleration-to-torque unit omission as741. Footer 16.

title: Lyapunov motivation and performance distinction
inspectionNotes: Energy-like positive function decreases along trajectories; stability without solving ODE. Stable not necessarily fast/good tracking. Wording will settle is too broad for mere Lyapunov stability; need asymptotic/invariance argument. Footer 17.

title: Linear mass-spring-damper energy
inspectionNotes: m xddot+b xdot+kx=0; v=1/2 m xdot²+1/2 kx²; derivative m xdot xddot+kx xdot=−b xdot²≤0. Rest kx=0 implies x=0 if k≠0. Require m,k>0 for positive definite energy and b>0 for dissipation. Derivative semidefinite in (x,xdot); asymptotic conclusion needs only invariant zero-derivative point, or positive-coefficient characteristic roots. Footer 18.

title: Direct method conditions and domain
inspectionNotes: Xdot=f(X), C1 positive-definite v with v(0)=0; vdot≤0 stability and <0 away from equilibrium asymptotic stability. Omitted equilibrium/regularity/local-domain qualification and compact-sublevel/properness for global boundedness. Cannot infer globally bounded state from arbitrary positive decreasing function alone. Footer 19.

title: Nonlinear spring-damper candidate
inspectionNotes: xddot+b(xdot)+k(x)=0 normalized mass. vdotnotation here v energy; nonlinear b and k functions NOT constant coefficients times arguments. Sign conditions xdot*b(xdot)>0 and x*k(x)>0 away0. Candidate v=.5 xdot²+integral0^x k(lambda)dlambda; negative x integral remains positive. Need b(0)=k(0)=0 and continuity/local-Lipschitz for usual equilibrium/invariance. Footer20.

title: Nonlinear derivative and invariant rest set
inspectionNotes: Derivative xdot[xddot+k(x)]=−xdot*b(xdot)≤0; zero when xdot0 need not imply x0 at instant. Right text erroneously For all trajectories xdot=0 and switches nonlinear k(x) to −kx; xddot=−kx also has nonzero moving solutions. Correct argument restrict trajectories remaining in zero-derivative set, then xdot identically0→xddot0 and b0=0→k(x)=0→x0. Footer21.

title: Why Does a Robot Need to See?

title: Introduction to Computer Vision
inspectionNotes: Vision described as inverse of graphics: 2D observations infer 3D world properties, whereas graphics renders 3D models. Desired properties shape, illumination and color distributions. Inverse does not imply unique reconstruction.

title: Introduction to Computer Vision (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: Projection loses depth; apparent size alone cannot distinguish size/distance. Figure contrasts human object labels Chair/Dog/Tree/Table with robot Feature extraction/Edge detection/Uncertainty and Object?; schematic is not a theorem that machines cannot recognize objects.

title: Fundamentals of Vision - Light
inspectionNotes: E(lambda) spectral intensity; medium absorption changes spectrum; slide attributes white-light dispersion to Newton in1670. Approximate visible range400–700nm. Plot normalized intensity versus wavelength300–1000nm: orange Sun5778K peaks around500nm; blue Lamp2600K rises across plotted interval, reaching its displayed maximum at1000nm. title: Human Vision
inspectionNotes: Printed L(lambda)=E(lambda)R(lambda) W m^-2, R in[0,1], diagram illuminant→surface reflectance→eye spectral response M(lambda). Simplified spectral product omits geometric radiometry and spectral-density units; use declared relative/discrete-band conventions in numerical examples. Rods more sensitive, intensity/night; cones daylight/color. Response integrates product of received spectrum and sensitivity.

title: Human Vision (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: Trichromatic compression into rho,gamma,beta with integrals L(lambda) times Mr,Mg,Mb. Upper normalized L/M/S curves overlap, peaks approximately570/545/445nm; L responds at medium as well as long wavelengths, not pure red-only channels. Lower plot shows three colored weighted spectral areas but no numbers defining exact integrals. Distinguish three responses from full spectrum.

title: Human Vision (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: Tristimulus value is3-vector rho,gamma,beta. Red-brick weighted spectral areas repeat lower plot from932; integrates areas, not just peak heights. Dominant L-cone response in this illustrated example, not an illumination-independent universal property of every red material.

title: Machine Vision - Digital Camera
inspectionNotes: Exact arrow pipeline: Real World → Optics (Lens/Aperture/shutter) → Sensor CCD/CMOS → Gain ISO → ADC → ISP Demosaic down to Denoise right to White balance up to Gamma right to Compress → RGB Image. Sensor chip encloses sensor/gain/ADC; photosites silicon regular array analogous to cones/retina. Ordering is the shown simplified pipeline, not a universal ISP sequence; sharpening/color correction added in later prose but not in diagram.

title: Digital imaging sensors
inspectionNotes: Actual figure contrasts CCD photon-to-electron in array, shifted charge to common charge-voltage conversion/output amplifier, versus CMOS pixel-local conversion and addressing. Prose CCD Charge-Coupled Device correct; CMOS expansion printed Complementary Metal Oxide on Silicon differs from standard semiconductor wording and must not be silently accepted. Simplified per-pixel amplifier description is a readout contrast, not proof of every commercial layout.

title: Machine Vision - Digital Camera (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: Color filter array above gray silicon photosites; colored Bayer grid has 2green/1red/1blue per2x2 tile, filters overlap spectrally. Gain ISO amplifies sensed signal before ADC; ADC converts analog voltage to discrete value. Gain does not collect extra incident photons; source exposure wording is simplified.

title: Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP)
inspectionNotes: Demosaicing estimates two missing color values per CFA pixel via neighbors, producing three color planes. Shot noise identified as photon-count variance, dark current as thermal electrons. Denoising reduces graininess especially low light. Sharpening edge enhancement compensates lens/demosaic blur; cannot assume perfect detail recovery.

title: Machine Vision - Image Signal Processor (ISP) (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: White balance channel gains aim for neutral equal RGB under illuminant changes. Color correction uses3x3 or3x4 C mapping camera responses toward CIE XYZ/sRGB because camera filters do not perfectly match cones. This color matrix C is not the later geometric3x4 camera projection matrix C. Gamma power-law encoding approximates perceptual/display response and is distinct from final JPEG compression; no exact gamma exponent or universal log law specified.

title: Geometric Image Formation - Image models
inspectionNotes: Actual diagram: light source illuminates a surface with normal n-hat; scattered rays include green ray through optics O to rear sensor plane. A separate virtual image plane is in front. Image formation maps 3D to 2D with depth loss; do not confuse physical rear sensor with front virtual plane.

title: Geometric Image Formation - Pinhole
inspectionNotes: Upright object left, small aperture middle, inverted smaller real image right. Ideal pinhole requires no focusing adjustment but transmits little light. Do not extend ideal ray model to unlimited sharpness or ignore diffraction when making physical claims.

title: Geometric Image Formation - Lens
inspectionNotes: Thin convex lens collects more light; diagram real upright object left and inverted real image right with focal points and equivalent pinhole. Printed 1/|zo|+1/|zi|=1/f applies to illustrated real-object/real-image distances; virtual-image calculations need an explicitly supplied sign convention. title: Perspective Projection
inspectionNotes: Virtual image plane f in front of camera center C gives non-inverted x=fX/Z and y=fY/Z. Camera axes and principal point shown. Require Z nonzero, and Z positive for visible front points under supplied convention. Homogeneous map is linear before division, ordinary perspective projection is nonlinear. Scale of a 3D point along a viewing ray is lost.

title: Perspective Projection - Camera Matrix
inspectionNotes: Homogeneous metric p=(fX,fY,Z), dehomogenized x=p1/p3, y=p2/p3. Homogeneous camera point (X,Y,Z,1); Cmetric=[[f,0,0,0],[0,f,0,0],[0,0,1,0]]. World point transformed into camera frame by inverse camera pose: CP=(OTC)^-1 OP. Actual diagram separates world O and camera C frames and point rays. Homogeneous scales and mixed units must be explained in calculations.

title: Perspective Projection (Cont.)
inspectionNotes: Sensor W by H pixels, photosite physical side lengths w and h. Upper-left pixel origin(0,0), u right and v down, last indices W-1/H-1. Principal point is optical-axis intersection, not necessarily pixel origin or exact sensor center. Positive x/y directions in virtual plane align with u/v in shown convention.

inspectionNotes: Principal point(u0,v0) is optical-axis intersection; u=x/w+u0, v=y/h+v0. title: Bayes Filter Algorithm
inspectionNotes: Bayes prediction integrates the motion model against the previous belief; correction multiplies by likelihood and normalizes. title: Belief Distributions - Gaussian Filter
inspectionNotes: Multivariate Gaussian density has an inverse and determinant normalization. Mean and symmetric covariance are shown, including all pose variances and cross-covariances. Covariance is a central second moment and is positive semidefinite; the ordinary full-dimensional density requires positive definiteness. Singular cases need separate support treatment. A single Gaussian is unimodal; a mixture is a different representation. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside extracted text.

title: Belief Distributions - Particle Filter
inspectionNotes: Particles are candidate states approximating a possibly multimodal, non-Gaussian belief. The graph places sample marks beneath a skewed curve. title: What is Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR)
inspectionNotes: ASR/STT maps acoustic speech to words or discrete text tokens. It is distinct from semantic interpretation and TTS. The waveform-to-text figure says “It’s time for lunch!” Modern systems may support language identification, translation, and speech-activity decisions, but multitask support does not imply every task is performed simultaneously on every call. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: How do robots understand speech?
inspectionNotes: Microphone converts acoustic pressure into an analog electrical signal; the diagram orders speech, microphone/waveform, ASR, text, language understanding, and robot action. Digital Signal is labeled after ASR, but digital processing also requires sampling/quantization before model inference. The analog voltage exactly mimics the acoustic shape only as an idealization of a real microphone transfer function. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Visualizing Speech as an Acoustic Waveform
inspectionNotes: Waveform axes are amplitude versus time, with a short approximately periodic segment from 0 to 0.03875 seconds. Amplitude relates to loudness under otherwise comparable conditions; repetition frequency relates to pitch, not a universal single-frequency description of all speech. Speech begins as varying air pressure and must be digitized for the illustrated processing. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stages in Speech Feature Extraction                                                                 DFT: Discrete Fourier
inspectionNotes: Feature pipeline figure: digitization, windowing/framing, DFT, log-Mel spectrum, then MFCC. Acronyms DFT and MFCC expanded. Output is a sequence of acoustic feature vectors. Whisper uses log-Mel input rather than requiring the final MFCC/DCT step; the entire pictured chain is not mandatory for every ASR model. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 1: Digitization
inspectionNotes: Digitization is sampling followed by quantization. Sampling gives discrete times at a rate such as 16 kHz; quantization maps measured amplitudes to finite levels, illustrated by 8- or 16-bit integers. Sampling alone does not quantize amplitude. Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate; a bandlimited signal and boundary/phase conditions are needed for accurate reconstruction, not the unqualified at-least-twice slogan. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 2: Windowing/Framing
inspectionNotes: Speech is nonstationary but short frames are treated as approximately stationary. The three window parameters are size, stride, and shape. Multiplication y[n] = w[n]s[n] selects and weights samples; it is not convolution. Window length and stride are different, allowing overlap. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 2: Windowing/Framing (contd.)
inspectionNotes: Rectangular and Hamming equations and both waveform plots inspected. The printed Hamming formula is 0.54 − 0.46 cos(2πn/L), 0 ≤ n ≤ L−1: a periodic convention, unlike symmetric denominator L−1. The claim that Hamming reaches zero at its boundaries is false: w[0] = 0.08. The prose calls L a number of frames although the formula indexes samples. Smooth curves illustrate already discrete sampled inputs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 3: Frequency Analysis
inspectionNotes: DFT equation X[k] = Σ x[n] exp(−j2πkn/N), n from 0 to N−1, and waveform-to-spectrum figure inspected. DFT gives complex magnitude/phase coefficients; FFT is an efficient algorithm for the same transform. The source uses a 25 ms Hamming-windowed frame and a frequency axis to 8000 Hz. Magnitude/power and dB scaling are later representations rather than the raw complex DFT itself. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 4: Mel Filter Bank & Log Spectrum
inspectionNotes: Overlapping triangular Mel filters are narrower and more closely spaced at low physical frequencies, wider at high frequencies. Their energy outputs form the Mel spectrum. The displayed convention is mel(f) = 1127 ln(1 + f/700), with f in Hz. This is one Mel convention, not all library defaults. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 4: Mel Filter Bank & Log Spectrum (contd.)
inspectionNotes: Each filter yields one scalar channel energy; the vector contains M channels. Logarithm is applied elementwise. The notation m_i refers ambiguously to filter and output energy; distinguish the weighted filter from its scalar response. Actual Whisper preprocessing also includes implementation-specific clamping, scaling, and feature-count conventions, so the generic log vector alone is not the exact numerical implementation. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Stage 5: Extracting MFCCs (Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients)
inspectionNotes: MFCCs capture a compact spectral-envelope/vocal-tract representation. A cepstrum plot shows amplitude against sample index. Overall energy and dynamic features are named, but these depend on whether energy and temporal delta features are included; a single static MFCC vector does not automatically contain temporal derivatives. Whisper uses log-Mel features instead of requiring MFCCs. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Traditional ASR pipeline
inspectionNotes: Traditional ASR: acoustic HMM–GMM model, pronunciation lexicon mapping words to phonemes, language model, and search decoder. The claim that every component is independently trained is too broad: a lexicon may be curated and a decoder is a search algorithm. End-to-end networks can combine modeling roles, but do not eliminate all preprocessing, search, or optional language-model integration. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Limitations of Traditional Systems
inspectionNotes: Sequence mismatch example: features every 10 ms, acoustic sequence 5 to 19 times text length. The ratio depends on tokenization, duration, and speech rate and is not universal. The Venn diagram places ASR at machine learning, signal processing, and NLP. Subsampling reduces length but alone does not solve variable speech/text alignment. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: CNNs for Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: One-frame temporal CNN illustration: z_j = x_j w_0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ t, with local dot products. The stride-one same-length statement is true for this one-frame case or suitable padding, not arbitrary valid convolutions. The scalar equation suppresses vector/channel dimensions. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: CNNs for Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: Odd-width kernel equation z_j = Σ from i=−p to p of x_(j+i) w_(i+p). Here p acts as half-width; equal zero padding can preserve length at stride one. Diagram shows padded edges and a three-weight kernel. A second equation sums channel convolutions but suppresses distinct per-channel weights and output channels. Stride greater than one reduces temporal length but need not skip every sample contribution or by itself solve alignment. Deep-learning Conv1d generally implements cross-correlation rather than weight-reversed mathematical convolution. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: Encoder-decoder diagram: 80-dimensional log-Mel frames, subsampling into shorter sequence X, encoder contextual output H, decoder receiving a start symbol and shifted previous text to predict “it’s time…”. Encoder listens and decoder generates one character or subword token at a time. This is the architecture shown, not a requirement for all ASR systems. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: Cross-attention uses Q from decoder hidden states and K,V from encoder acoustic representations. Equations Q=H_dec WQ, K=H_enc WK, V=H_enc WV and softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V inspected. Diagram includes encoder self-attention, decoder causal self-attention, decoder cross-attention, normalization, feedforward layers, residual paths, and a language-modeling output head. Cross-attention is standard in encoder-decoder Transformers, not a new addition unique to speech. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: Causal decoder self-attention uses prior text, unlike acoustic cross-attention. Greedy decoding selects the highest conditional next-token probability and feeds that token back. The source uses characters as an illustration; modern tokenizers may use subwords. Local greedy choices do not guarantee the highest joint sequence probability. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.

title: Transformer-Based Speech Recognition
inspectionNotes: Autoregressive product conditions every term on audio and earlier tokens, although the displayed left side omits the conditioning on X. Scoring is literally log P(Y|X)/|Y|_c + λ log P_LM(Y): only the acoustic term is length-normalized, not the whole sum. External LM influence is controlled by λ. This is an example scoring rule, not proof that default Whisper decoding uses external LM fusion. Actual 1800×1013 pixels inspected alongside text.
